meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

watches.desc: Watches follow one operational thread of an item on its own once a trigger event makes it worth it, as a record of tactical lessons: which tactics and actions succeeded, which failed and which were superseded, on both sides, with dated evidence. Two kinds: a shadow-war watch (kind "shadow-war": sabotage, incursions, cable damage, jamming and other attacks below the threshold of war, and the defenders' countermeasures) and an operation watch (kind "operation": one named military operation). Each carries a narrower daily feed, plus dated findings and an assessment researched from open sources at each review.

types.succeeded: The tactic or action achieved its aim, on the evidence available (ground taken and held, target hit, intrusion undetected or unanswered, threat intercepted, cell caught before acting).
types.failed: The tactic or action did not achieve its aim or was defeated (attack repulsed, objective abandoned, intruder shot down, perpetrators caught with little effect).
types.superseded: The tactic or plan was replaced by a newer method or made obsolete by a countermeasure (a plan scaled back, a weapon or approach overtaken).
types.contested: The outcome is unclear or disputed: claims not yet confirmed, sources disagree, or it is too early to judge.

items.whyNow: The strike war spread beyond the theatre this week: Ukraine sank the corvette Merkury at Benghazi on 22 Nov with sea drones launched from western Libya, and Russian missiles and drones crossed into Poland on 20, 23 and 24 Nov. With the Kerch road link still down and Putin conceding on 24 Nov that refinery strikes are a substantial burden, attacks on logistics and energy, not the static ground front or the stalled guarantee talks, are setting the winter terms.
changes: 26 Nov: Trump urged Putin to 'pull back all military aggression' across Europe after Russian missiles and drones entered Polish airspace on 23–24 Nov and called a deal a 'strong possibility'; a large outage hit occupied Crimea, where power restrictions from 25 Nov could last up to 10 days (Kyiv Independent).

25 Nov: Ukraine hit the Kuibyshev and Syzran refineries in Samara Oblast (15 refineries struck in November) and reported its first laser interception of a jet-powered Geran; its General Staff said a strike on Savasleyka air base damaged three MiG-31s and two Su-34s; Russian strikes cut power in five oblasts and the Zaporizhzhia NPP lost external power for the 17th time this year (ISW).

24 Nov: Haftar's Libyan National Army said two of its naval officers died of wounds from the Benghazi attack and vowed retaliation; Putin acknowledged Ukrainian oil strikes are a substantial financial burden as Russia imposed fuel export restrictions (Al Jazeera; AP; ISW).

23 Nov: Zelensky confirmed seven Ukrainian sea drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at Benghazi on 22 Nov and destroyed its Ka-27 helicopter, with the cargo ship Angara also hit; Ukraine halted the Novoshakhtinsk refinery, and Peskov said Moscow awaits Kyiv's reply on a Kostiantynivka 'humanitarian' pause (ISW; Al Jazeera).

22 Nov: Russia launched 186 drones and about 20 glide bombs on Zaporizhzhia city; Ukrainian forces advanced south-east of Dobropillya against fog-covered mechanised assaults; Ukraine's navy said Russia has no viable substitute for the Kerch road link and forecast Crimean shortages from about 29 Nov (ISW).

21 Nov: Zelensky widened his proposed localised ceasefire along the Dnipro and said NATO membership was being discussed with Washington and Europe, a day after Russia's deputy foreign minister Ryabkov called accession 'unacceptable' (ISW; Kyiv Independent).

timeline.text: Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, setting fires at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and Ruchi depot and hitting a VK data centre about 850 km from the border, its deepest mass raid of the war.

A limited humanitarian ceasefire around occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast took effect for aid deliveries and evacuations, the first agreed local truce of the year, while Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles and 280 drones.

Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones, all the missiles aimed at Kyiv and its region, hitting the city's Northern Bridge four times and a substation linking two nuclear plants to central Ukraine.
US-mediated trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi ended after two days with agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange but no ceasefire and no movement on territory.
A second night of Ukrainian drone and missile strikes collapsed a road span and arch of the Kerch Bridge, halting road traffic between Russia and occupied Crimea while rail service continued.

Russia fired 27 ballistic missiles, 84 cruise missiles and 404 drones overnight, its largest strike of November, killing eight and damaging three Dnipro bridges in Kyiv, while Russian missiles and drones came down in Poland.

Seven Ukrainian sea drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya, wounding ten people; two Libyan naval officers later died and Haftar's army vowed retaliation.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status is borne out: Russian forces again used fog to cover mechanised assaults near Dobropillya on 22 and 25 Nov, yet ISW recorded Ukrainian advances south-east of Dobropillya on 20 and 22 Nov and no Russian gains near Kostiantynivka or Hulyaipole on 24–25 Nov, so weather still buys windows rather than ground. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising status is reinforced from both directions. Ukraine sank the corvette Merkury at Benghazi on 22 Nov with seven sea drones launched from western Libya, carrying uncrewed strike far outside the theatre, and reported a first laser kill of a jet-powered Geran on 25 Nov, still in testing, while US Patriot deliveries stayed held and Russia kept sending 64–76 jet drones a night.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the Established and Contested status is shifting against Russia: one Kerch rail track reopened on 19 Nov but the road section remains destroyed, Ukraine is hitting the M-14 land route, and Putin conceded on 24 Nov that refinery strikes are a substantial burden. Russia's deliberate re-striking of repaired Ukrainian power lines on 23 Nov mirrors the method, so attacking repair cycles, not single nodes, is what both sides now test.

watches.question: Which Russian tactics below the threshold of open war against Europe (drone and aircraft incursions, sabotage and arson through recruited proxies, undersea cable and pipeline damage, shadow-fleet operations, GPS jamming, cyber attacks with real-world effect) are succeeding, which are failing or being countered, and which have been superseded; and how are European and NATO countermeasures (air policing and counter-drone defence, rules of engagement, maritime interdiction, arrests and expulsions) adapting?

findings.tactic: Arrests and expulsions as sabotage deterrent
findings.text: An IISS report released on 26 Nov 2026 finds explosive and arson attacks roughly doubled over the past year, with Germany and Poland accounting for more than half of incidents from Oct 2025 to Sep 2026, and recruited proxies moving to timed improvised explosive devices. It concludes there is no clear evidence that arrests, expulsions of intelligence officers and consulate closures have made sabotage less attractive to the Kremlin, and that disrupting one proxy network may not stop competing ones; this is the think tank's assessment, not a measured result.

Dragonfly data reported on 25 Nov 2026 count 194 suspected Russia-linked sabotage incidents in the first eight months of 2026, up 62% year on year, with half of incidents from June to September aimed at military or defence-industrial sites. Russian state officers carried out 64% of incidents before 2022 but fewer than one in ten since 2024: after mass expulsions of intelligence officers, direct state action has been superseded by locally recruited proxies, often criminals or people hired online, which obscures attribution (one firm's count).

findings.tactic: Ship-borne GPS jamming over the North Sea
findings.text: Reported on 25 Nov 2026: aviation intelligence group Hexbird traced GPS interference on 9 Nov, lasting about 20 minutes and affecting an estimated 140 flights including British Airways, Ryanair and easyJet services, to a point about 190 miles off England where a Russian warship was escorting three cargo ships. Hexbird neither confirmed nor ruled out the convoy as the source, NATS received no pilot reports and the flights saw no operational impact, while the UK government declined to comment; the attribution remains a claim.

Late on 23 Nov 2026 a Russian drone, reported by PAP to be a jet-powered reconnaissance type, briefly entered Polish airspace during a night attack on western Ukraine. Radar tracked it throughout and commanders cleared a shoot-down, but held fire when it turned east, citing risk to civilians from debris, so the incursion again went unintercepted; Poland is now preparing a no-fly zone along its eastern border, which a deputy minister hopes takes effect in late December or early January.

findings.tactic: Intercepting Russian missiles over Ukraine; AWACS reinforcement
findings.text: On 23 Nov 2026 Poland asked allies in Brussels to consider shooting down Russian missiles over Ukraine when they head for NATO territory, which Sikorski called self-defence, but Deputy Defence Minister Tomczyk said NATO is 'in no way favorable' and Romania reportedly balked. The same day NATO authorised a forward AWACS deployment to Poland while not answering the request for allied F-35s, so the forward-defence idea is stalled and the added surveillance is untested.

findings.actor: Unidentified drones (Finnish military says likely Ukraine)
findings.tactic: Drone strike on Russian military cargo ship
findings.text: On the morning of 21 Nov 2026 drones struck the Sparta II, operated by Russian defence-ministry contractor Oboronlogistika and bound for Kaliningrad, west of Suursaari; it burned and drifted into Finnish waters near Loviisa, the crew was evacuated and Finland warned it could sink and imposed air and sea restrictions. Ukraine has not claimed it, though a Finnish military spokesman said Ukraine was likely responsible; a Russian helicopter allegedly entered Finnish airspace up to 4.1 km during the response, which Finland is investigating.

On the night of 19-20 Nov 2026 Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles and a suspected drone crossed into south-eastern Poland during a mass strike on Ukraine and came down in rural areas without casualties; neither Polish nor allied forces shot any down, and a Swedish Gripen pilot cleared by NATO held fire because thick cloud hid the missile. Poland summoned the Russian ambassador and asked for AWACS and F-35 reinforcement, conceding that the existing air-policing posture did not stop the overflight.

findings.actor: Polish government, police, Border Guard and army
findings.tactic: Public threat disclosure and border surge
findings.text: Rzeczpospolita reported on 18 Nov 2026, citing government and intelligence sources, that the plot Poland's 2-15 Nov Kaliningrad-border operation was guarding against was never executed; special services coordinator Siemoniak would not confirm a false flag but said the deployment answered a real threat. ISW assesses that Tusk's public warnings and the surge of police, counter-terrorism and army units likely deterred or disrupted the operation, an assessment rather than proof of deterrence.

findings.tactic: Drone overflights of Moldova during Ukraine strikes
findings.text: On the evening of 17 Nov 2026 seven drones violated Moldovan airspace, one flying over Chisinau according to President Sandu; the defence ministry said five crashed near villages, a sixth possibly in Ocnita and a seventh vanished from radar near Leova heading for Romania, and civilian flights were briefly suspended. No drone was reported shot down, so the incursion again achieved disruption without interception; Russia denies its drones enter Moldova.

findings.tactic: Arresting contract saboteurs and closing border
findings.text: Estonia's chief prosecutor said on 15 Nov 2026 that eight Latvian residents had been detained over the Threod Systems attack, which Prime Minister Michal attributed to Russian intelligence, and Tallinn announced it will close its border crossings with Russia from 1 Dec. The swift arrests contained the attack; whether closing the crossings stops recruitment of disposable proxies from third countries is untested.

findings.tactic: Drone strikes on merchant ships off Sulina
findings.text: Late on 13 Nov 2026 drones hit the cargo ship Larissa 1 and late on 14 Nov the tankers Evia Petrol V and Ali Najafov and the bulk carrier Marsol near Romania's Sulina canal, two of them inside Romanian territorial waters; fires were put out and no one was hurt, Reuters reported. ISW calls Evia Petrol V the first NATO-flagged vessel struck; the strikes landed despite two fighter scrambles, while the drones' origin is unconfirmed and Russia denies targeting Ukraine's neighbours.

findings.actor: Russian intelligence (per Estonian PM); eight Latvian-resident proxies
findings.tactic: Explosive arson attack on drone maker
findings.text: In the early hours of 14 Nov 2026 an attempt to cause an explosion and fire hit Threod Systems, a drone maker near Tallinn, following the August arson at Milrem Robotics. PM Michal said heightened security and a swift police reaction averted extensive damage and the attackers were detained; the GRU attribution rests on Estonian officials, who have not shown their evidence.

assessment.text: From 13 to 27 Nov cheap stand-off tools kept working while Europe's air defences held fire. Kh-101 missiles crossed Poland on 19-20 Nov with nothing shot down (a Gripen pilot held fire in cloud) and a Russian reconnaissance drone left on 23 Nov after commanders cleared but withheld a shot over debris fears, echoing unintercepted drones over Moldova (17 Nov) and off Sulina (13-14 Nov). Defenders are adapting slowly: NATO authorised an AWACS for Poland on 23 Nov and Warsaw plans an eastern no-fly zone, but its call to down missiles over Ukraine met NATO resistance. Close-in sabotage is still often foiled, as at Threod Systems on 14 Nov, yet IISS (26 Nov) finds explosive and arson attacks doubled with no clear deterrent effect from arrests and expulsions, while Dragonfly data show state officers superseded by disposable local proxies. At sea the contest is widening: a suspected warship jammed GPS off England (claim) and drones burned a Russian military cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on 21 Nov.

text: Long-range strike versus integrated air and missile defence (Established · Contested) is borne out, with the defence leaking at the margins: Iran fired missiles and drones at Patriot radars in Bahrain on 21 Nov, where one strike reached an industrial site at Sitra, and on 26 Nov a drone strike on a Kuwaiti air-defence station killed two Italian technicians, so high interception rates no longer mean no casualties. timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.

The Hague conciliation round closed with the first agreed confidence-building measures (a direct channel between the two navies among them, by Thailand's account), while the Commission noted earlier measures were unimplemented and set a third meeting in Kuala Lumpur for 24–27 November.

Thailand's defence minister said the boundary dispute was unresolved, parked defence-ministry talks in favour of the Regional Border Committee, and said troops facing Cambodian soldiers climbing Hill 642 apply rules of engagement starting with dialogue and warning shots.

The ASEAN Observer Team visited the Chey Chomneas checkpoint area in Pursat, where Cambodia said Thai forces had moved an observation post about 20 metres forward and kept digging trenches, and the team inspected a bridge destroyed by Thai airstrikes in December 2025.

Hun Manet opened the Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh by calling the ceasefire fragile and proposing a Francophone mediation network, and the summit closed on 16 November with leaders backing Cambodia's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said he had warned Hun Manet that Thailand would halt all other bilateral talks, including joint demining and land boundary demarcation, if Cambodia kept pursuing compulsory maritime conciliation.

Cambodia said Thai forces built a new fortified bunker at Boeung Trakoun in Banteay Meanchey and brought in road machinery the next day, after a Thai official visit with journalists to the An Ses area of Preah Vihear on 19 November.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving status holds only for shooting: no exchange of fire or mine casualty was found from 13 to 26 Nov, but the tools that manage incidents are eroding. Anutin said on 21 Nov that joint demining and demarcation stop if Cambodia keeps pursuing compulsory conciliation, and Kao Kim Hourn warned on 24 Nov that bilateral channels are idle and a third round of fighting is possible. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the reinforcement trigger is close to firing: Cambodia says Thai forces built a new bunker at Boeung Trakoun on 21 Nov and brought road machinery on 22 Nov (Cambodian account), Thailand defended a 19 Nov official visit to An Ses as within its deployment lines, and Thai public donations of about 269 million baht are funding fences and bunkers. Fortification is becoming civic as well as military.

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the Background monitor status is contradicted: Thailand is using the land track as leverage against the UN conciliation that sat from 24 Nov, while Washington listed Thailand's intent to buy HIMARS on 18 Nov. Mediation now leans on Singapore's 2027 chair. Adaptability stays Low.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the watch-for-trigger status holds with the trigger dormant: no strike on Venezuelan soil was found after the 30 Oct Apure raid, and the sovereignty question now sits inside the 18 Nov cooperation agreement, whose text is unpublished. Defence Minister González López said on 18–19 Nov that cooperation will respect the constitution and that the armed forces keep command of their operations, a public limit on any US footprint. On border and maritime control versus illicit networks, the Established status is borne out but quiet: InsightCrime's tally shows no lethal boat strike since 27 Oct, and Colombia’s president had denied by 19 Nov a New York Times report that Bogotá had rejected joint operations on its soil, saying foreign troops would need congressional approval.

On information operations versus political legitimacy, the Rising status is borne out: the fourth round closed on 23 Nov with eight procedural points but no electoral council, election date or prisoner deal, while Foro Penal counts 321 political prisoners. Security integration with Washington is outpacing electoral reform, which is the legitimacy gap to watch at the 10 Dec round. Adaptability stays Medium.

timeline.text: Three PLAN warships, including two Type 022 missile boats, and five China Coast Guard cutters intercepted the MV Lapu-Lapu resupply run about 60 nautical miles from Second Thomas Shoal, a warship radioed that it would take 'compulsory measures' and the mission was suspended, the first blocked run since the July 2024 understanding.

The carrier Liaoning and three destroyers sailed through the Sulu Sea and the Basilan Strait inside the Philippine archipelago, shadowed by Philippine warships, before heading east toward the Philippine Sea, as Chinese navy ships near Philippine-held features rose to 26 in the week to 26 October.

China's Southern Theater Command said its naval and air forces flew combat-readiness patrols around Scarborough Shoal as a countermeasure to Philippine 'provocations', a day after a Philippine patrol flight found an unidentified Chinese vessel with a sensor-fitted craft inside the shoal's lagoon.

ASEAN and China failed to conclude the South China Sea code of conduct at the Manila summit despite about 80% of the draft being agreed, leaving its legal force and geographic scope to Singapore's 2027 chairmanship.
Satellite analysis reported by AFP showed China building a runway of nearly three kilometres on Antelope Reef in the Paracels, its second in that group and expected to be usable by mid-2027.

A Chinese militia vessel closed to about 200 yards of the coast guard ship BRP Cabra and chased its inflatable boat as the coast guard drove two anchored militia vessels away from Loaita Cay, in a week when Chinese vessels at four Philippine-claimed features rose from 19 to 48.

text: On grey-zone maritime coercion versus presence and resilience, the Established · Contested status is borne out and the post-summit pause proved short: a week after the 16 Nov self-restraint pledge, a Chinese militia vessel closed to about 200 yards of BRP Cabra and pursued a coast guard inflatable at Loaita Cay on 23 Nov, and the armed forces counted 48 Chinese hulls in the week to 23 Nov against 19 the week before. The militia, not the coast guard, carried the pressure at a Philippine-held feature, an incremental shift that keeps contact below the threshold of a state response. On maritime domain awareness versus ambiguous attribution, the Rising status holds: Manila again published hull counts and named the militia hull, and Beijing's 26 Nov warning to Tokyo over planned radar and drone transfers shows that the sensing aid itself is now contested.

On distributed maritime posture versus force protection, the Rising · Contested status is reinforced: five PLA Navy warships sat at Scarborough Shoal in the week to 23 Nov, and on 26 Nov Beijing pledged 'firm' measures against Australia's new arrangement with Manila on maritime activity and defence infrastructure, while patrolling jointly with Vietnam's navy on 20-21 Nov, which separates claimants it pressures from those it engages. changes: 26 Nov: A Houthi projectile hit the Jazan refinery, killing a Nepali worker, injuring several others and suspending some operations; the coalition said it destroyed the ballistic-missile launch platform at Hodeidah port used in the attack, and Saudi air defences downed two ballistic missiles over Riyadh and two drones over the Eastern Province (Arab News, The National).

25 Nov: After renewed coalition strikes on Hodeidah port, a Houthi projectile hit Jizan port causing minor damage, a drone was intercepted near Jeddah Islamic Port, and the Houthis claimed the Ras Tanura refinery, where satellite imagery showed heavy smoke while the coalition reported only four drones intercepted (Al Jazeera, The National, Critical Threats).

24 Nov: A second strike in five days on the Public Investment Fund tower in Riyadh's financial district wounded 11 people; Saudi aircraft struck Hodeidah port and Houthi positions near the Taiz–Aden road, and satellite imagery showed a Houthi-dug moat south of Jabal Kharaz, which Critical Threats reads as a defensive posture on the Lahij front (Critical Threats, The National).
